subject: Banking
title: Collections and Your Score
description: A quick win: understand Collections and Your Score.

hook.text: A debt sent to collections drops your credit score 100+ points. One in four Americans has a debt in collections.

buildup.text: After 120-180 days of non-payment, the original lender gives up and sells your debt to a collection agency for pennies.

discovery.text: Collection agencies buy debt for 4-7 cents on the dollar. If they collect even 30%, they make enormous profit margins.

twist.text: Medical debt and paid collections are treated differently now, so not every collection hits the same.

climax.text: Collections punish people twice: the financial burden of the debt plus the credit score damage that blocks future.

punchline.text: Bought for 4 cents. Collected for 30 cents.

quiz.question: How much do collection agencies pay for debt?

details.summary: When debts go unpaid for 90 to 180 days, creditors sell them to collection agencies that aggressively pursue repayment. A collections entry on your credit report is one of the most damaging events possible, dropping scores by 100 points or more.
details.whyItMatters: Collections affect nearly one in three Americans with credit files. Understanding the collections process helps avoid the devastating credit impact and navigate the aggressive but regulated tactics that collection agencies use.
takeaways: Debts are sold to collectors for pennies on the dollar after 90 to 180 days
A collections entry can drop your credit score by over 100 points
Medical debt collections rules have recently become more consumer-friendly

faq.question: Can you negotiate with collection agencies?
faq.answer: Yes. Since agencies buy debt for pennies on the dollar, they are often willing to settle for less than the full amount. Pay-for-delete agreements, where the agency removes the entry from your report in exchange for payment, are also possible.

faq.question: How long do collections stay on your credit report?
faq.answer: Seven years from the date of first delinquency with the original creditor. The impact on your score diminishes over time, and recent changes have removed paid medical collections from credit reports entirely.
